source_refs.note: Book p. 231: 12.3.1 One-Sided Limits: opening paragraph, '(i) The Left Hand Limit', 'The Right Hand Limit' (no '(ii)' printed) and the Note side box on the rules for one-sided limits.

blocks.text: In defining \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\), we restricted \(x\) in an open interval containing \(c\), i.e., we studied the behaviour of \(f\) on both sides of \(c\). However, in some cases it is necessary to investigate one sided limits, that is, the left hand limit and the right hand limit.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why would we look at one side only? Three common situations:
1. The function is given by different formulas on the two sides of \(c\) (a piecewise function), e.g. \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) for \(x \le 2\) and \(7 - x\) for \(x > 2\). Each side must be worked out with its own formula.
2. The function behaves differently on the two sides, e.g. \(\frac{|x|}{x}\) is \(-1\) for every \(x < 0\) and \(1\) for every \(x > 0\).
3. The function exists on one side only, e.g. \(\sqrt{x}\) near \(x = 0\) is defined only for \(x \ge 0\).

\(\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = L\) is read as the limit of \(f(x)\) is equal to \(L\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\) from the left, i.e., for all \(x\) sufficiently close to \(c\), but less than \(c\), the value of \(f(x)\) can be made as close as we please to \(L\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The small minus sign in \(c^{-}\) does not mean a negative number. It means "from the left", i.e. through values smaller than \(c\). For \(c = 3\): \(x\) takes values like \(2.9, 2.99, 2.999, \dots\) and comes closer and closer to 3 without reaching it.

\(\lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = M\) is read as the limit of \(f(x)\) is equal to \(M\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\) from the right, i.e., for all \(x\) sufficiently close to \(c\), but greater than \(c\), the value of \(f(x)\) can be made as close as we please to \(M\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book numbers the left hand limit as (i) but prints no "(ii)" before The Right Hand Limit; the right hand limit is simply the second of the two one-sided limits.
Here \(c^{+}\) means "from the right": for \(c = 3\), \(x = 3.1, 3.01, 3.001, \dots\)

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The rules for calculating the left hand and the right hand limits are the same as we studied to calculate limits in the preceding section.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to find a one-sided limit in practice:
1. Decide which side you are on: \(x < c\) for \(c^{-}\), \(x > c\) for \(c^{+}\).
2. Pick the formula of \(f\) that is valid on that side.
3. Evaluate the limit of that formula with the usual rules (substitute; if you get \(\frac{0}{0}\), simplify first).
Example (ours, not from the book): \(f(x) = \frac{|x|}{x}\) at \(c = 0\). For \(x < 0\), \(|x| = -x\), so \(f(x) = -1\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} f(x) = -1\). For \(x > 0\), \(|x| = x\), so \(f(x) = 1\) and \(\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} f(x) = 1\). The two one-sided limits are different; in 12.3.2 we will see what that means.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Always write the side in the subscript (\(x \to 2^{-}\) or \(x \to 2^{+}\)) and say which formula you used, e.g. "for \(x < 2\), \(f(x) = 2x + 1\)". Examiners give marks for choosing the right piece.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Left hand limit \(\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x)\): \(x\) comes close to \(c\) through values less than \(c\).
2. Right hand limit \(\lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x)\): \(x\) comes close to \(c\) through values greater than \(c\).
3. The rules are the same as for ordinary limits; only the side (and so the formula) changes.
4. The value \(f(c)\) itself plays no part in either one-sided limit.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(c^{-}\) as "negative \(c\)": \(x \to 2^{-}\) means \(x\) approaches \(+2\) from below, not \(-2\).
2. Using the wrong piece of a piecewise function: for \(x \to 2^{+}\) use the formula written for \(x > 2\), even if another formula is written for \(x \le 2\).
3. Putting \(f(c)\) in place of a one-sided limit; they can be different.
